Thank you for the question. Distinguished colleagues, representatives of member states and partners. CTED's mandate under Security Council resolutions on counterterrorism places us at the intersection of legal obligation and operational reality. CTED has performed 209 country assessments to 120 member states. Each country assessment gives us a granular, evidence-based picture of where implementation gaps exist. And I want to use this time to speak directly to what those assessments tell us about air cargo security and what they demand of us collectively. Resolution 1373 is unambiguous. States are required to prevent and suppress the financing of terrorist acts, deny safe haven,— and critically for today's discussion, take the necessary steps to prevent the commission of terrorist acts, including through the prevention of illicit cross-border movement of goods. Resolution 2309 goes further, explicitly recognizing civil aviation as both a transport vector and an attack surface for terrorist groups, and obliging states to prevent illicit good flows through aviation by strengthening security systems screening, inspection, risk management, specifically through ICAO mechanisms. Resolution 2370 of 2017 is dedicated to preventing terrorists from acquiring weapons, including explosives and IEDs and their components. Uh, there we go. What our assessments reveal is a persistent and troubling implementation gap between these obligations on paper and the operational realities on the ground. Let me be specific about the nature of that gap. First, on screening architecture, many states have adopted the ICAO Annex 17 framework in their national aviation security programs, but implementation of the cargo security standards, particularly Standards 4.6 through 4.8 concerning security controls for cargo and mail prior to aircraft loading remains inconsistent. Our assessment shows that a significant number of states do not yet have functioning regulated agent regimes with robust chain of custody controls. Cargo is cleared not because it has been screened, but because it has passed through a known cosigner relationship that in practice lacks the verification protocols and ANIX 17 contemplates. This is a structural vulnerability. Second, on advanced cargo information and risk profiling, the exploitation of pre-departure data, such as cargo manifests, airway bills, shipper declarations for intelligence-led targeting remain underdeveloped in many jurisdictions. UNODC's PCCP has made significant inroads in building customs capacity to use advanced electronic information for risk stratification. But we consistently see that the interface between customs risk analysis units and civil aviation security authorities is weak or absent. There are separate bureaucratic silos operating on the same cargo flows with minimal data sharing architecture between them. From a counterterrorism standpoint, that is an exploitable seam. Third, and that is the threat dimension that warrants serious attention, our assessments have documented a pattern of attempts to conceal improvised explosive devices and improvised incendiary devices within cargo and airmail shipments. These are not hypothetical scenarios. The operational challenge these incidents pose is not primarily one of detection technology. Such as X-ray and CTX systems are reasonably well deployed at major hubs, but it's of risk-based targeting, identifying which of the millions of daily cargo consignments warrant secondary examination. Without functioning intelligence-led targeting, screening becomes statistically random rather than risk-based, and that is insufficient against a determined adversary with knowledge of cargo workflows. Fourth, on strategic trade and export control. Resolution 2370 of 2017 provides CTED with the broader mandate of covering all weapons, including explosives and IED components. Our assessments show that export control frameworks in many states do not adequately cover dual-use transiting through air cargo or CBRN-applicable precursors moving through free trade zones adjacent to international airports. The firearms and parts component, including the trafficking of disassembled weapons through postal and courier channels, remains a significant gap in many regional contexts. Fifth, on terrorist travel and the civil aviation nexus. Under the UN Countering Terrorist Travel Program, The threat assessment models capability co-established by UNOCT and ICAO provides member states with a structured methodology for intelligence-led threat assessments in civil aviation. CTED's recommendations consistently urge states to ensure they conduct full and systematic risk management processes, keeping in mind the effectiveness of interagency cooperation. CTED's assessments have underscored that passenger side security has advanced significantly since the post-2001 architecture was built through PNR collection, API data, and watchlist screening. But cargo side threat assessment is a decade behind in terms of systematic intelligence-led methodology. We need to close this gap, and the TAM Framework provides a vehicle for doing so. So this brings us to what does CTED recommend operationally? We urge member states to conduct explicit mapping exercises between their national aviation security programs and their customs risk analysis frameworks, identifying where information sharing protocols are absent and establishing them, not as a matter of courtesy between agencies, but as a legal implementation requirement under Resolution 2309. We recommend that states building or reforming their regulated agent regimes do so with supply chain traceability as the organizing principle, meaning that the integrity of a consignment must be verifiable from point of origin to aircraft loading with documented break of chain protocols that trigger enhanced screening. We call on member states to institutionalize interagency cooperation and information exchange exchange mechanisms. And we urge engagement in building national threat assessment processes for cargo and mail that are genuinely intelligence-led, drawing on financial intelligence, watchlist data, and pattern of life analysis on freight forwarders and logistic intermediaries, not simply reactive and physical screening anomalies. CTED stands ready to support member states in and through its mandate to facilitate technical assistance in translating these recommendations into concrete legislative and administrative action. Our technical assessment visits provide a structured mechanism for identifying specific implementation gaps, and our legal and policy tools are available to support that work. The threat is technical, and the response must be equally so. Aviation cargo security is not a peripheral concern within the counterterrorism agenda. It is a central vulnerability that well-resourced terrorist networks and transnational organized crime groups are actively seeking to exploit. Our collective obligation is to close the gaps they are mapping. Thank you.

And something that we have put out there is, uh, we want to express our final risk score in Canadian dollars. So our consequences are all financially based. Now, we could sit here and argue about the absolute dollar costs of a plane going down. This is a relevant model, right? And so as long as we come to some type of an agreement on generally speaking what the attack would do and those hypothetical destructive and disruptive costs, the relevant nature of the varying scenarios still comes into, clarity. So our threat assessment, uh, considers intent to carry out a specific type of attack and the capability, feasibility of carrying out said attack. Um, this is very much driven on intelligence, the intent part, but also history of attack. I mean, all of us understand in the world of aviation security and counter-terrorism that there is hist— history of attack types against civil aviation, but we don't have a huge amount of data sets necessary necessarily to, to point to. A lot of this is driven on chatter. A lot of this is driven on an understanding of what some of the big players may be wanting to do against the aviation system, or in some cases against the transportation system at large. And some of these are just being, you know, pieces put together, certain products being purchased, um, certain suggestive elements within intelligence to try to guide our understanding of what some of these, uh, malicious actors may want to do to the system. The second component is the capability feasibility. It's the reasonable capacity of a malicious actor to su— to su— uh, to successfully carry out an attack. Uh, so this can be simply stated as, you know, if I am a malicious actor and I want to go to the airport and I wanna stab some people, it is pretty easy for me to go to my kitchen, pull out a knife, and drive to the airport and be successful in that attack path. It is more difficult to build an IED to do so. It is more difficult to build an IED that I feel may be successful in circumventing a pre-board screening system. So there is a, a granularity, uh, in, in the way in which that we look at these things. Obviously subject matter expert informed. We have bomb experts within Transport Canada that help support important understanding of the different types of bombs that could be brought into the system, as well as incendiary devices through cargo, to really hone in on what the capability feasibility of an average actor could be to, to be able to do these things, not only in the physical nature of building these things, but also in the aptitude of the average individual to learn the approach. This is, as noted, assessed in collaboration with government security and intelligence partners, not just domestically but also internationally. Um, this is an intelligence-led process. If there's no intelligence for us necessarily to, uh, to say that's— that there's malicious actors, uh, that have an intent to do something, we try to do our best not to get too focused on it. We want to ensure that overarching intelligence is the driver of our risk-based approach. I've highlighted there reasonable worst-case scenario. This is another area in which things can get carried away. We're not talking about, uh, a malicious actor jumping out of a helicopter with an IED on his back and slapping it on the side of a moving aircraft. Uh, we are talking about the reasonable real world. I understand none of us saw 9/11 coming, um, but we have to play within the ballpark as best we can, obviously allowing for our intelligence as best we can to understand the system that we are up against. Consequences as well, reasonable worst-case scenario. We're not talking about, you know, another 9/11 necessarily, but an aircraft likely hitting a stadium or a major, a major building in a major city. Vulnerability evaluates the likelihood that an attack would be successful if attempted. This is an evaluation of the presence or absence of security measures and controls along said attack pathway. The effectiveness of those controls as well, once again on a scale of 0 to 1. So within our public areas of our airport, you have CCTV, you have the occasional walk-by of some type of a law enforcement individual, but it is not the same level of security measures as making its way to the aircraft itself, right? So something like the Belgian attacks, an attack on IED with firearms, it is much easier for a malicious actor to pull that off than actually making its way to an aircraft itself. This also takes into consideration our national compliance rates, understanding not, you know, speaking to the effectiveness of our system as well. Consequences are evaluated in terms of the degree of destruction, disruption, and harm to people expressed in Canadian dollars. A relative cost estimate of consequences of each scenario is assessed using what we have is a value of statistical life. I want to make sure that we are not saying how much a person's life is worth. Uh, it is a cost-benefit analysis number. It doesn't matter what number you use necessarily, as long as it is consistent. So on an average aircraft leaving Canada, making its way over the Atlantic, it's approximately 225 people on board.— that's 225 people that would be passed if, if that incident was to occur, as well as the cost of the aircraft and the general disruption costs. Also, in conjunction, this data set is built on not only Canadian information, but also it's supported by our Five Eyes partners and an understanding of our Five Eyes partners with respect to that data. Reasonable worst-case scenario, once again, Calculating said risk, the score of threat on a 0 to 1 scale, vulnerability on a 0 to 1 scale, and the consequences in dollars are therefore multiplied, arriving at a final risk score. So risk is threat times vulnerability times consequence. For example, 0.4 times 0.75 times a billion dollars, risk equals $300 million. That is also put on a low, medium-low, medium, medium-high, high scale to inform senior management direction as well. That's all, folks.

So based on that, we had to find a way to respond to this challenge in a practical way by first establishing a joint approach to help these communities, you know, build that relationship. And it really is about generally trying to explain at first what the other side is doing, to clear any myths about sometimes what the intelligence community can or cannot do, and also importantly identify value points for the other side. Next, it's key for those two communities to start establishing clear communication channels and protocols. Institutionalizing the relationship really does help building, you know, this routine and reinforces the informal that shouldn't be left on its own, but that's necessary to kind of smoothen the processes. And then lastly, the icing on the cake, feedback mechanism is really key to help you know, both the producing side and the consumer side to align and get to work in a way that is more efficient and to bring more quality to your products. But I think it's fair to say that we can transfer some of that to cargo security. So next slide, please. So I said what TAM does really is to help states develop their own national frameworks for threat information sharing in the context of civil aviation. That is left to the actual information holders, right? We're here to help build that kind of framework through which you can channel information. It's also important to find a way, you know, to develop a framework that makes sense in the local environment. You know, not all frameworks will work in the same place. So if we look at some of the key factors that allow for switching to this analytics-driven approach, some would say intelligence-led approach, there are really 3 that I'd like to highlight tonight. The first one being that It all starts with identifying your producing forces on the one side and your consumer base on the other side. When you talk about a threat assessment, you start by identifying your stakeholders, get them to understand their roles and responsibilities, their value in the chain. It may sound obvious, but effective cooperation on aviation security requires a comprehensive all-inclusive approach encompassing multilateral exchange between the counter-terrorism community, government authorities, civil aviation regulatory authorities, and operational-level industry stakeholders. Don't overlook them, they have a lot of information, lots of expertise as well, that operates within around the state's aviation ecosystem. And by that I mean the security screening system providers, postal services, the freight forwarders, the shippers, even the insurers might have something to say about risk. So all of these people, it's important to hear what they have to say and find a way, you know, to kind of bring that information together in a way that makes sense. The second piece to that slide is that through the program, we're trying to bring those, you know, core stakeholders around the table to spend time to discuss, you know, how best to develop a national interagency framework that really works for everyone. We find that set frequency for assessments is key.
